content: Primary fallopian tube cancer (PFTC), commonly referred to as tubal cancer, is a malignant tumor that originates in the fallopian tubes. Tubal cancer is considered a rare form of primary gynecologic cancer, accounting for approximately 1 to 2 percent of all gynecologic malignancies. In the United States, the incidence of tubal cancer was reported to be 0.41 cases per 100,000 women between 1998 and 2003. The demographic distribution of tubal cancer is similar to that of ovarian cancer, with the highest incidence observed in white, non-Hispanic women and those aged 60 to 79 years. However, recent studies suggest that tubal cancer may be more common than previously thought. Evidence indicates that individuals with BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations are at a significantly higher risk of developing PFTC. The most prevalent histological type of tubal cancer is adenocarcinoma. In a large study involving 3,051 cases, 88% of the tumors were classified as adenocarcinomas. Among these, approximately half were poorly differentiated, 89% were unilateral, and the distribution of disease extension was roughly one-third each for local, regional, and distant spread. Less common types of tubal neoplasms include leiomyosarcoma and transitional cell carcinoma. Due to the close anatomical relationship between the fallopian tubes and the ovaries, it is often the pathologist, rather than the surgeon, who determines whether the tumor originates in the fallopian tube. Secondary tubal cancer typically arises from primary cancers of the ovaries, endometrium, gastrointestinal tract, peritoneum, or breast. The internal anatomical location of the fallopian tubes makes early diagnosis challenging. Symptoms are often nonspecific and may include pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, or abnormal vaginal bleeding. A pelvic mass may sometimes be identified during a routine gynecologic examination. Vaginal discharge associated with fallopian tube carcinoma is often due to intermittent hydrosalpinx, a condition referred to as hydrops tubae profluens. A pelvic examination may reveal an adnexal mass, which can raise suspicion for tubal cancer. The CA-125 blood test, while nonspecific, is frequently elevated in patients with tubal cancer. More definitive diagnostic tools include gynecologic ultrasound, CT scans, or MRI of the pelvis. Occasionally, early-stage fallopian tube cancer is discovered incidentally during pelvic surgery performed for other reasons. The primary treatment for tubal cancer is surgical intervention, which is similar to the approach used for ovarian cancer. Surgery typically involves a total abdominal hysterectomy, which includes the removal of the uterus, cervix, ovaries, and fallopian tubes. Additional procedures include peritoneal washings, omentectomy, and sampling of pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes. The stage of the disease, determined during surgery and through pathological evaluation, guides subsequent treatment decisions. In advanced cases where the cancer has spread extensively and cannot be completely resected, cytoreductive surgery is performed to reduce the tumor burden and facilitate further treatment. Surgery is usually followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, most commonly platinum-based regimens. Radiation therapy has also been used in some cases, either for palliative purposes or with curative intent. Staging of fallopian tube cancer is performed according to the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) staging system during surgery. The prognosis for patients with fallopian tube cancer is largely dependent on the stage of the disease at diagnosis. In 1991, it was reported that approximately 50% of patients with advanced-stage disease survived for five years when treated with surgery followed by cisplatin-based chemotherapy.
